articles.title: ‘It was all of us’: Khawaja says entire Australia team knew about sandpaper ball tampering plot
articles.summary: Former Test opener says object also used on cricket ball in Port Elizabeth. CA remains ‘comfortable’ with bans only for Bancroft, Warner and Smith. Usman Khawaja has claimed “all” of the Australia touring party knew about the plot to tamper with the ball against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018…
body: The former Australia batter said the team used sandpaper to tamper with the ball before Cameron Bancroft was caught on camera while handling the object during the third Test, ahead of the release of Khawaja’s autobiography Sabr on Tuesday.

Bancroft, David Warner and Steve Smith were the only players sanctioned after a Cricket Australia investigation found the trio had prior knowledge of the scheme to use sandpaper as a ball tampering agent in Cape Town.
Captain Smith and Vice-captain Warner were suspended for 12 months for their parts in the plot, while Bancroft was handed a nine-month ban for using sandpaper on the ball.
“It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us,” Khawaja says in his book, according to Nine newspapers.

articles.title: Thierno Barry double fires Everton to comeback win against Coventry
articles.summary: The most optimistic Evertonian – if that is not an oxymoron – could not have envisaged David Moyes’s team sitting fifth in the Premier League and Thierno Barry just behind Erling Haaland in the goalscoring chart at the end of the club’s calamitous transfer window.
body: The wildly optimistic Evertonian – if such a being exists – could not have envisaged David Moyes’ side fifth in the Premier League with Thierno Barry just behind Erling Haaland in the goalscoring chart when their transfer window closed in calamitous fashion. Yet there they sit, team and striker defying all expectations, following a stirring comeback against luckless Coventry.

Frank Lampard endured a torturous night against his old club as Coventry impressed but were refused two strong penalty claims. The Coventry manager felt his team were denied a third time by the video assistant referee for an apparent handball by Barry when edging Everton ahead. Replays were inconclusive. It was the dancing French forward’s second goal of the game and tenth in all competitions this season. He also delivered a fine assist for Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall as the in-form midfielder put his latest England disappointment behind him to seal victory in convincing style.

articles.title: USA women throttle Switzerland 7-0 to open hockey worlds amid jersey dispute
articles.summary: Bilka and Edwards score twice each in American rout. Canada open with 5-1 win over Sweden as Eldridge shines. Jersey dispute overshadows tournament’s Danish debut. The United States opened their defense of the women’s ice hockey world championship with a 7-0 victory over Switzerland on Friday in…
body: Hannah Bilka and Laila Edwards scored twice each, while Kirsten Simms, Hilary Knight and Casey O’Brien also found the net as the Americans pulled away after a competitive opening period. Caroline Harvey contributed three assists.

Bilka broke the deadlock nine minutes into the game, but Switzerland goaltender Andrea Brändli kept the favorites at bay for the remainder of the first period. The Americans took control in the second, with O’Brien doubling their lead before Edwards converted a power play just 15 seconds after a Swiss penalty.
The US outshot Switzerland 15-3 in the second period before adding four more goals in the third, including Bilka’s second and a solo effort from Simms.

Knight, the United States’ longest-tenured player making her 16th world championship appearance, scored midway through the final period to extend her tournament records to 68 goals and 121 points in 88 games. The 37-year-old is the competition’s all-time leader in both categories.

articles.title: Charlton’s struggles expose ‘absolute ocean’ between WSL and second tier
articles.summary: Pointless after eight games, Karen Hills’ team are struggling to compete against clubs with chunkier wallets. Played eight, lost eight. Welcome to the Women’s Super League, Charlton Athletic, a club in danger of being chewed up, toyed with and spat straight back out by the top tier.
body: Bruised by their 6-0 defeat against Chelsea on Sunday, last season’s playoff winners are finding WSL life tough, conceding more than three goals per game on average and struggling to compete against clubs with chunkier wallets. But are they underperforming or are they merely the victims of their own success?

Promoted against the odds last season, defying some of the bigger-spending sides in the second tier such as Newcastle and Bristol City, Karen Hills’ team overachieved by eventually beating Leicester on penalties to secure a top-flight spot. And that was the last time they had anything to cheer about. Sunday’s trip to second-bottom Crystal Palace, another of the promoted sides, theoretically offers Charlton one of their better opportunities to match the 2026 UK Eurovision entry Look Mum No Computer and register one point.

articles.title: WTA chair apologises to Pegula after 'diva' comment broadcast
articles.summary: Audio recording on practice courts will be deactivated at the WTA Finals after private comments made by Jessica Pegula about Mirra Andreeva were picked up, with the governing body's chair apologising to the American for the "regrettable" incident.
body: US player Pegula describing Russian teenager Andreeva as "a diva" while conversing with coach Mark Knowles during a practice session were heard on a YouTube livestream at Indian Wells, the venue for the WTA Tour season-ending event from November 8-15.

The WTA shouldered the blame for failing to properly inform players about active microphones, with chair Valerie Camillo saying there was "a lack of advanced notice and clear signage" as she confirmed audio will now be switched off for practice sessions.
Camillo added: "I want to specifically apologise to Jessica Pegula and [coach] Mark Knowles. What happened was regrettable and unacceptable.
"Jess is one of the WTA's best advocates and biggest stars. She does not deserve this distraction.

articles.title: Lampard: VAR didn't do its job
articles.summary: Coventry boss Frank Lampard says VAR 'didn't do its job' in his side's defeat to Everton as three reviews controversially went against his side.
body: Two penalty appeals and a possible handball for Everton's second goal were all reviewed by VAR officials Timothy Wood and Gary Beswick, but nothing was given. They were also not awarded on-field by referee Stuart Attwell.
Coventry opened the scoring after the two penalty appeals, but were ultimately beaten 3-1 on Merseyside on Friday Night Football.
Lampard told Sky Sports: "I hate to sound like a moaner. It's a football match and if you win the game, that can happen here. I've worked here and know the momentum swings in the game.
"I'm not trying to talk about the circumstances of the actual football, but when big decisions change games, they absolutely do. It's disappointing. VAR is there for that and it didn't do its job."

articles.title: Leclerc plans 'significant' car changes after tough day for Ferrari
articles.summary: Charles Leclerc says he will make "significant" setup changes to his car after "one of the worst feelings" in practice at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.
body: Leclerc was seven tenths off pace-setter Kimi Antonelli in second practice and Lewis Hamilton was nearly half a second behind as Ferrari trailed Mercedes, McLaren and Red Bull on Friday.

It was a contrast to their recent pace with Ferrari claiming a podium position in the last four races but Leclerc is hoping they can turn that around in final practice on Saturday at 2.30pm and qualifying at 6pm, live on Sky Sports F1.
"FP2 was very tricky. Actually, if anything, one of the worst feeling I've had this year in the car, so there's plenty to work on, and it didn't feel quite right," said Leclerc.

"I've got some ideas. We'll change the car quite significantly, and we'll see how it goes. I hope we can do a step forward because even though I missed FP1, I don't think there was much performance in that.

articles.title: Fritz misses out on ATP Finals after squandering chance to beat Alcaraz
articles.summary: Taylor Fritz missed out on claiming the last spot at the ATP Finals in Turin later this month after squandering two match points in his Paris Masters quarter-final defeat to Carlos Alcaraz.
body: Fritz would have reached the end-of-season event in Italy at Rafael Jodar's expense had he beaten Alcaraz to make the last four.
He looked poised to do that after twice finding himself a point from victory in the second set, once on his opponent's serve at 5-3 up and then on his own with the score at 5-4.
However, Alcaraz rallied during a high-quality match to triumph 6-7 (10-12) 7-5 6-3 and ensure he will be joined by compatriot Jodar at the ATP Finals from November 15-22, live on Sky Sports.

Tommy Paul's three-set defeat to fellow American Ben Shelton earlier in the day - US Open finalist Shelton prevailing 6-4 4-6 6-3 - had ended his hope of reaching the ATP Finals, with countryman Frances Tiafoe's place subsequently secured.

articles.title: ‘Stop playing games’: SEC reportedly considering luxury tax for schools that overspend on players
articles.summary: The SEC might be borrowing an idea from professional sports. The conference is reportedly considering a luxury tax on schools that spend more on their players than the revenue-sharing cap allows.
body: A working group of SEC athletic directors, university presidents, and general counsels has been discussing the idea for the past few weeks. The league could vote on it soon, with the hope of having it in place before football’s early signing period in December.

Under the House v. NCAA settlement, schools are allowed to pay their athletes directly through revenue sharing, up to a set cap. That cap is $21.3 million for the 2026-27 academic year and will rise to about $22.2 million in 2027-28.

Schools have found ways to spend beyond that, though. Much of the extra money gets routed through third-party NIL deals, which makes it hard for anyone to know what their competitors are actually paying.

The SEC isn’t the only conference trying to rein that in. Last month, the Big Ten adopted a conference rule limiting its schools’ involvement in third-party NIL deals, ahead of the possible passage of the Protect College Sports Act in Congress. The PCSA would increase the amount schools can pay players directly by $27.5 million. It’s now unclear whether Congress will pass it after Tuesday’s elections.
points: The SEC might be borrowing an idea from professional sports.
The conference is reportedly considering a luxury tax on schools that spend more on their players than the revenue-sharing cap allows.
That cap is $21.3 million for the 2026-27 academic year and will rise to about $22.2 million in 2027-28.
The PCSA would increase the amount schools can pay players directly by $27.5 million.
